# One system to run the phone, the field, the money and the marketing

URL: https://alphaflux.net/
Section: Platform

AlphaFlux puts the whole operation behind one login and one customer record. A call becomes a lead, a lead becomes a job, a job becomes a recurring agreement, and nothing gets typed twice.

## One system to run the phone, the field, the money and the marketing

A customer calls. The call is logged, the address is geocoded, the job is booked against real capacity, the technician is routed, the proof is captured, the invoice goes out and the follow-up email writes itself. All of that is one record moving through one platform.

Most service companies run a phone system, a field service tool, a CRM, an email tool and a spreadsheet, then pay someone to keep the five of them in agreement. AlphaFlux is the alternative: every module reads and writes the same customer, the same job and the same money.

Every job carries its own record: customer, technician, route, proof, payment and notes. Open it once and you see all of it.

- Scheduled (06:40)
- Dispatched (07:05)
- On site (07:52)
- Complete (08:31)

## Three numbers that describe the shape of it

- 1: One platform in place of a phone system, a field service tool, a CRM, an email tool and a spreadsheet.
- 20: What the free plan covers, at one location, permanently and without a card.
- 3: Anything you can do on screen you can also do over the API or hand to an AI agent with a scoped key.

## Five systems means five copies of the same customer

The phone system knows the number. The field tool knows the address. The CRM knows the deal. The email tool knows the list. Nobody knows the whole story.

That fragmentation is expensive in a way that is easy to miss. Someone becomes a full time translator between systems. Jobs get booked against capacity nobody can see. A customer who moved is still getting mail at the old address in one tool and not another. A technician arrives without knowing the account is ninety days overdue.

AlphaFlux keeps one record and lets every module work on it. The dispatcher, the technician, the office manager and the owner are all looking at the same customer, in the same state, at the same time.

- One customer record: Created by the phone call, enriched by the job, billed by the agreement, emailed by the campaign. Never duplicated.
- One definition of capacity: A booking is checked against real capacity before it is confirmed, so the schedule cannot be oversold by a person or by an agent.
- One version of the money: Payments, invoices, recurring agreements and commissions all read from the same ledger, in integer cents.
- One timeline per account: Calls, texts, emails, notes, AI activity and payments in a single chronological feed.

## Eleven modules, one login

Each module can be switched on or off per company. You only see and only pay for what you actually use, and adding one never means migrating your data.


## A job is a record, not a text message

The order strip below is the same object every module works on. The dispatcher moves it, the technician moves it, an agent can move it, and the customer sees the result.

- Scheduled (06:40)
- Dispatched (07:05)
- On site (07:52)
- Complete (08:31)

## Your agents get a key, not your password

AlphaFlux was built assuming a machine will do a growing share of the work. Every capability is an interface first, and a screen second.

Issue a scoped API key and an agent can book jobs, send texts, run billing, chase overdue accounts or write back to the account timeline, and it can only do the things that key allows. Turn a key off and the agent stops, without a password ever changing hands.

The receptionist answers the phone before a person does. The assistant answers a technician's question about a treatment. Autopilot lets an agent keep a company's configuration tidy. Every action is attributed, so you can always tell what a machine did and what a person did.

- Scoped keys: Read and write, per module. A key inherits exactly the permissions of the account that owns it.
- A command line that speaks JSON: Every command outputs JSON, so it pipes into a script or straight into another agent turn.
- An MCP server: Point any agent client at it and the whole platform becomes a set of tools it can call.
- Attribution on every action: Notes and sales record whether a person, an agent or an import did the work.

## Built for the way the work actually arrives

Nobody calls at a convenient time, and nothing in a service business stays still. The platform assumes both.

- The phone answers itself: An AI receptionist handles the call, books against real capacity and hands a human the rest. Missed calls get a text back automatically.
- Recurring work runs itself: Agreements generate their own visits for the length of the term. Monthly recurring revenue is calculated from the actual charges, not from a guess.
- Stock follows the truck: Inventory is not one warehouse. It is trucks, storage units, mobile units and branches, with sign in and sign out and a record of who has what.
- Dispatch is a map and a board: See every job and every technician live, drag work between stages, sequence a day route, and let the customer watch their technician arrive.
- Email marketing from your own domain: Campaigns, sequences and a unified inbox, sent from your domain with the authentication records handled for you.
- Your data stays on your machine: Self-hosted, per company isolation, and an audit trail on every change. Nothing is sold, shared or used to train anything.

You should not have to buy five products, and then buy a person to hold them together.


## What the free plan covers, and what moves you up

The free plan is a real plan, not a trial. It is free permanently, and it is designed for someone running the business out of a truck.


| Price | !Free forever | $49 per month | $149 per month | $399 per month |
| Customers | 20 | 250 | 1,000 | 5,000 |
| Locations | 1 | 2 | 5 | 15 |
| Users | 1 | 3 | 10 | 25 |
| Marketing emails | 100 per month | 2,000 per month | 10,000 per month | 50,000 per month |
| Phone numbers | 1 | 2 | 5 | 25 |
| Inventory and custody | yes | yes | yes | yes |

## Start in an afternoon, not a quarter

- Create the account: An email address is the whole signup. No card, no sales call, no implementation fee. The free plan is available immediately.
- Bring in what you already have: Import customers and inventory from a spreadsheet, or connect an existing field service account and read it live while you decide what to move.
- Turn on the modules you want: Start with the phone and the schedule. Add dispatch, fleet, marketing or agent access when the work needs it.

### Is the free plan really free, or is it a trial?

It is free permanently. Twenty customers, one location, one user, one phone number, 100 marketing emails a month and the inventory module are yours for as long as you want them. There is no card on file and no expiry date. Companies move up when their workload outgrows those limits, and when they do, everything they have already entered comes with them.

### What does one location mean?

A location is a base you operate from: a city, an office or a service area. If a company works out of one town, that is one location and everything fits on the free plan. A company running crews in three states needs three, which is what the paid plans are for.

### Do I need to install anything?

No. AlphaFlux runs on infrastructure the platform provider hosts and keeps running, and every module works in a browser on a laptop, a tablet or a phone. The technician view installs to a phone home screen like an app and keeps working when the signal drops.

### Can an AI really be trusted to run parts of this?

It can be trusted with exactly as much as you give it. An agent authenticates with a scoped key, so it can only reach the modules and the operations that key names. Every action it takes is written to the audit trail and to the account timeline, attributed to the agent rather than to a person.

### What happens to my data if I leave?

It is yours and it exports. Customer records, jobs, invoices and payment history come out in standard formats, including a full JSON export through the API. Nothing is held hostage and nothing is deleted without an explicit request.

### Does AlphaFlux work for a company with more than one branch?

Yes, and branches are modelled properly rather than treated as a naming convention. Each location has its own staff, its own schedule, its own capacity rules and its own stock. Roles can be scoped to a location, so a dispatcher in one district cannot see or change another.

# One platform, eleven modules, one customer record

URL: https://alphaflux.net/platform
Section: Platform

AlphaFlux is not eleven products bolted together. It is one system with a registry of modules, a single data model underneath, and three interchangeable ways to drive it.

## Modules are switched on per company, not per installation

Every feature area ships as a module with a stable identity. A company sees the modules it has and nothing else.

That matters for two reasons. First, a company that answers the phone, books the work and invoices it does not have to look at fleet telematics or chemical registers it will never use. Second, turning a module on later never means a migration, because the module was always reading the same records the rest of the platform already keeps.

Modules are grouped into bundles so pricing stays legible, and any single module can be added to any plan as an add on. The catalogue, the bundles and the limits are all data, which is what makes white labelling possible: the whole catalogue can be repackaged under another brand.

- A registry, not a menu: Each module declares its own identity, the limits it enforces and the permissions it needs. The screen is generated from that registry rather than hard coded.
- No cross-module coupling: Modules work on shared records through defined interfaces, so one can be replaced without touching the others.
- Bundles and add ons: A plan is a set of modules plus limits on customers, locations, users, volume and storage.
- Limits that announce themselves: Approaching a limit is visible before it is hit, and hitting one never destroys data. It stops the next thing from being created.

## How your data is kept separate from everyone else's

Multi-tenant software earns trust by being specific about what separates one company's records from another's. Here is exactly what does.

- Tenant scope on every record: Every domain row carries the company it belongs to, and every query is scoped to the company of the account making the request. There is no code path that returns a record outside your scope.
- Scoped credentials, hashed at rest: API keys are stored only as a hash and shown once at creation. Provider credentials, such as a phone carrier token, are write only and are stripped out of every response, including the ones that echo them back.
- Roles and departments: A role is a named set of permissions. A department is a slice of the company, such as a district or a line of service. A role can be scoped to a department, so a dispatcher in one office cannot see another office's work.
  - Owner, administrator, office manager, dispatcher, technician, billing, marketing, support, and read only auditor
  - Permissions are explicit per capability rather than implied by a job title
  - Restricted actions are refused by the server and the reason is named in the response
- Isolation you can upgrade: Records are currently separated by tenant scope inside one store, which keeps operations simple and cost low. A dedicated store per company is a configuration change rather than a rewrite, because every data access goes through one internal interface.
- Where it physically runs: Self-hosted on a machine the operator controls, behind a TLS terminator with automatic certificates. Backups are encrypted before they leave the host.

## Three ways to drive the same platform

The screen, the API and an agent are three clients of one thing. Nothing is available in one and missing from another.

This is the design decision that separates AlphaFlux from software that bolted a chat box onto an existing interface. Every capability is an interface first, which is why an agent can do real work here rather than summarising a dashboard.

It also means you are not locked into a single way of working. A manager uses the board. An ops lead scripts a nightly report. An agent answers the phone at nine at night. The same records change either way.

- The screen: A console for the office and a mobile view for the field, both generated from the module registry and the permissions of the person signed in.
- The API: A documented REST interface with a machine readable specification, so an integration can be written against it without a conversation.
- The command line: A single binary that talks to the same API and prints JSON, for scripts, cron jobs and pipelines.
- Agent access: A protocol server that presents the platform to an AI client as a set of callable tools, authenticated with a scoped key.

## The engineering choices a buyer should care about

None of this is visible on screen, and all of it decides whether the platform is still fast and correct in year three.

- Fast by construction: A small compiled service per component, no framework layered on top, and no third party script running in your browser. Pages and lists stay quick as the data grows.
- Money in whole cents: Prices, payments, splits and recurring revenue are stored as whole cents and basis points. There is no floating point arithmetic anywhere near an invoice.
- Callbacks verified when they arrive: Inbound carrier webhooks and provider callbacks are checked before they are acted on, so a forged request cannot create a job or move money.
- An audit entry on every change: Who acted, under what role, on which company, doing what, at what time. Readable by the owner, filterable by an agent.
- Idempotent where it counts: Recurring visit generation, campaign sends and imports are safe to run twice. A retry never bills a customer twice.
- Built to be left alone: Scheduled work, retrying jobs and health checks run without supervision, and a person is alerted when something needs one.

If the platform is doing its job, nobody should be copying and pasting between two tabs.


## What happens when a module goes live

- The catalogue changes, not the data: Enabling a module registers its screens, its permissions and its endpoints. The records it needs already exist because the customer record is shared.
- Limits attach to the company: The plan sets what the module is allowed to grow to. The module enforces those limits itself rather than trusting the interface.
- Permissions appear for the roles you choose: Enabling a module adds new available permissions. Nothing is granted automatically, so nobody gains access because a feature was switched on.
- History starts now, and it is complete: From the first day a module is on, its actions appear in the account timeline and the audit trail alongside everything else.

### Can I run more than one company on one installation?

Yes. One installation serves many companies, each with its own records, users, modules, limits and branding. That is the same mechanism white labelling uses, so an operator can run their own business and their customers' businesses side by side.

### What happens when I reach a limit on my plan?

The platform stops the next record from being created and tells you which limit you reached and what plan lifts it. Nothing is deleted, nothing is hidden, and nothing you have already entered becomes read only. Raising the plan takes effect immediately.

### Can I use just one module?

Yes. Some companies start with the phone module and nothing else, because that is the part that is losing them money. Modules can be added one at a time as the need appears.

### Is there a mobile app?

The field views install to a phone home screen and work offline, which covers the technician case without an app store. Camera capture, signatures and location reporting all work from the browser, and status changes made without signal are queued and applied when the connection returns.

### Do I need a server?

No. AlphaFlux runs on infrastructure the platform provider hosts and maintains. Self-hosting on your own hardware is available for organisations that require it, and it uses the same components.

# Give an agent a key, not your password

URL: https://alphaflux.net/ai-agents
Section: Platform

Most software added a chat box that can talk about your data. AlphaFlux was built the other way round: every capability is an interface first, so an agent can do the work and not just describe it.

## The receptionist answers before a person has to

A call comes in at 9pm on a Friday. Nobody is in the office. The phone is still answered, the caller is still helped, and the job is on the board before Monday.

The receptionist answers first, with a fifteen second timer. If it handles the call, a human is never rung and the caller never knows the office was closed. If it cannot, the call rolls to the person on duty, or to voicemail with an automatic text back, according to the rule you set for that number and that hour.

What it can do is bounded on purpose. It can identify the caller, work out which office serves their address, check whether the service they are describing is one you offer, book an appointment against real capacity, take the details and leave a complete record. It cannot invent a price, promise an exact arrival time, or book a job that would oversell a technician's day.

Its script is versioned inside the platform rather than hidden in a vendor's dashboard, so changing how your phone is answered is an edit you make, not a support ticket you file.

- Hour aware: Different behaviour inside and outside business hours, with a rule per number.
- Territory aware: It resolves the address to the correct office and respects the areas you do and do not serve.
- Capacity aware: A booking is checked against real capacity before it is confirmed, so an agent cannot oversell a day.
- Escalation that works: Emergencies are routed to a person immediately, and a solicitor gets a scripted answer rather than a technician's time.

## What an agent can do on day one

Concrete work, not demonstrations. Each of these runs against the same records your staff use.

- Answer, book and tidy up: The receptionist takes the call and books the visit. An agent then confirms the slot against capacity, texts the customer the window, and writes a note on the account marked as agent authored.
- Chase a missed call: Read the missed call, look up the number, send the text back, open a follow up note, and raise a ticket if the customer replies. If they book, the ticket closes itself.
- Run the money: Compute the period's usage, apply the agreed margin, issue the invoice, read the payment run, and flag the accounts that have gone past terms with the amount and the age of the debt.
- Work the board: Read today's jobs, flag the ones a technician cannot reach in time, re-sequence a route, and notify the affected customers with a new window.
- Keep the records clean: Find duplicate accounts with the evidence that links them, propose the merge, and apply the ones a person approves. Nothing merges on its own authority.
- Report upward: Pull the operating numbers, compare them with the previous period, and produce a short written digest with the two or three things that changed.

## How the access actually works

An agent is a credential with a job, not a person with a password. Everything about the design follows from that.

- A scoped key: Read and write access is granted per module. An agent that books jobs does not need, and does not get, the billing module.
- Inherits its owner, and nothing more: A key carries exactly the permissions and the companies of the account that created it. It cannot reach past its owner.
- Revocable without a reset: Disable a key and the agent stops working. No password changes, no disruption for the humans on the system.
- Everything is an endpoint: The agent connects over the same documented interface your other software would, so nothing it does is special or unreviewable.
- Attributed, always: Records carry whether a person, an agent or an import made a change. Sales, notes, tickets and jobs all record it.
- Autopilot, if you want it: A per company switch lets agents keep configuration tidy and heal small problems on their own, under the same attributions and the same audit trail.

## Why attribution is the part that matters

Once an agent handles a meaningful share of the work, the first question an owner asks is not whether it is fast. It is which of these did a machine do, and can I see the difference.

AlphaFlux records the actor on every action, and it distinguishes an agent from a person from an import. Revenue an agent booked is separable from revenue a person booked. A note written by the receptionist reads as agent authored. A ticket the assistant raised says so on its face.

That is also what makes the numbers trustworthy later. When commission is calculated, when a customer complains, when a regulator asks who touched a record, the answer is already in the data rather than reconstructed from memory.


The difference between an agent you trust with real work and one you do not is whether the platform can say no in a structured way.


## Guardrails, stated plainly

- No raw database access: An agent works through the same validated operations your software uses. There is no path from a model to an arbitrary query.
- No credentials in a prompt: Agents receive what they need to answer and act. Payment tokens, carrier credentials and full customer records are not put in front of a model.
- Confirmation where it matters: Proposals are separated from actions. A merge, a price change or a bulk send asks a person to confirm before anything is written.
- A trail you can read: Every action lands in the audit log with actor, role, company, action and time, readable by the owner and filterable by an agent.

### Do I have to use AI at all?

No. Every module works fully with people driving it. Agents are an additional way to operate the same records, and they can be switched off entirely without changing how anything else behaves.

### What stops an agent from doing something expensive?

Three things. The key only carries the permissions it was issued. The platform refuses operations that break a rule regardless of who asked, such as a booking that would exceed a day's capacity. And the operations that carry real consequence, like merging accounts or issuing a bulk send, are presented as a proposal that a person confirms.

### Which AI providers can it use?

AlphaFlux is provider agnostic. It can run against a hosted model of your choosing or against a model running on your own hardware, which is the arrangement that keeps customer data inside your building.

### How do I connect an agent?

Issue a scoped key in the console, then hand the key to the agent. For agent clients that support tool protocols, the platform presents itself as a set of callable tools, so the agent discovers the available operations rather than being told about them. Developers can read the developer page for the exact interfaces.

### Can an agent email my customers?

Yes, through the email marketing module, under the same suppression list and consent rules a person is held to. A customer who has unsubscribed is excluded from an agent's send exactly as they are from a person's.

# Every module in the registry

URL: https://alphaflux.net/modules
Section: Platform

Eleven modules, one customer record, one login. Switch on what a company needs, leave the rest off. Nothing here requires a migration to adopt later.

## The modules

Each one works on its own and gets better when the others are on, because they all read and write the same records.


## Which plan carries which module

Bundles set the floor. Any module can also be added to any plan on its own.


| Phone and messaging | 1 number, 1 user | 2 numbers, 3 users | 5 numbers, 10 users | 25 numbers, 25 users |

## Turning a module on is a configuration change

There is no separate database per feature and no import step between them. A module is a view onto records the platform was already keeping.

That is why a company can start with the phone and the schedule, add dispatch three months later, and add fleet after buying its first truck, without any of it being a project.

It is also why reports stay honest as modules appear. The numbers were always being recorded, so history does not start over when a new module is switched on.

- Registry driven: Screens, permissions and limits all come from the module registry, so the interface matches what a company actually has.
- Permissions do not grant themselves: Turning on a module makes new permissions available. Someone still has to assign them, so nobody gains access by accident.
- History is continuous: A module that starts today reads work that was recorded before it existed. Nothing has to be backfilled.
- Repackageable: Because the catalogue is data, an operator running the platform under their own brand can define their own bundles and pricing.

## Modules that pair well

Some combinations are the reason the platform exists. These are the ones companies turn on first.

- Phone plus scheduling: The agent answers, checks real capacity and books, so the schedule fills itself instead of waiting for office hours.
- Field operations plus inventory: A job draws down the technician's stock, and a low part is visible before the next job needs it rather than after.
- Fleet plus reports: Distance, on time percentage and jobs per technician come out of the same records the dispatcher is already using.
- Billing plus agreements: Recurring visits and recurring revenue are one object, so the invoiced amount and the booked work cannot drift apart.
- Email plus CRM: A campaign targets a real pipeline stage, and a reply lands on the account timeline rather than in a separate list.
- Anything plus agent access: Hand an agent a scoped key and it can work across modules under one set of permissions and one audit trail.

### Can I buy a module without the bundle around it?

Yes. Any module can be added to any plan as an add on, priced on its own. That is usually how a company moves up: it adds the one thing that is currently costing it money rather than changing plan.

### What happens if I switch a module off?

It stops appearing and its operations stop being available. The records it produced are not deleted, and switching it back on restores access to all of it.

### Is there a module for something you have not built yet?

The registry is open. New modules follow the same contract as the existing ones, so adding one does not disturb the others, and the interface picks it up without a redesign.

### Do the modules share one database?

They share one data model, which is the point. Records are scoped to the company that owns them rather than to the module that created them, so the customer your phone module logged is the customer the dispatch board routes to.

# Access you can explain to someone who asks

URL: https://alphaflux.net/security
Section: Platform

Security questions are usually answered with adjectives. Here are the actual mechanisms, including the ones that are inconvenient.

## How signing in works

The largest single cause of account compromise is a password reused somewhere else. The most reliable fix is not to have one.

- Email or text one time codes: A person signs in by receiving a short lived code. There is no password to reuse, to forget, to share or to find in a breach dump, because there is no password.
- Codes that expire and limit attempts: A code is valid for a short window, is stored only as a hash, allows a small number of attempts, and cannot be requested again immediately. Guessing is not a realistic path.
- Sign in that does not reveal who has an account: An unrecognised address receives the same response as a recognised one, so the sign in page cannot be used to enumerate your customers or your staff.
- Server side sessions that rotate: A session is a server side record rather than a token the browser holds data in. It rotates on sign in, is destroyed on sign out, and can be invalidated centrally.
- Rate limiting on the way in: Repeated failed attempts from one source are slowed and then refused, which is what turns a brute force attempt into a nuisance rather than an incident.

## Credentials are treated as radioactive

The dangerous data in a platform like this is not the customer list. It is the keys that can move money and send messages.

Carrier credentials and provider tokens are write only after they are stored. They are never returned by the interface, and they are stripped out of the responses that echo them back, because several providers hand your own credential straight back to you in a response body and a naive proxy would pass that on.

Keys that agents use are stored only as a hash and are displayed exactly once, at the moment they are created. If a key is lost, it is replaced, not recovered, because a system that can show you a key again is a system an attacker can ask the same question of.

The same rule applies on the way out. When the platform calls a provider, credentials travel in headers the provider expects and are never placed in a URL where they would end up in a log.

Every action taken with a key is recorded against the account that owns it, so a compromised key has a name, a scope and a timestamp rather than an unknown blast radius.

- Write only secrets: Stored and usable, never readable back to a person or an API caller.
- Scrubbed responses: Upstream replies that contain your own credentials have them removed before the reply reaches you.
- Hashed API keys: Shown once at creation and stored as a hash. Revoking is immediate and auditable.
- Every key has a name: An action is attributable to the credential and to the account that issued it.

## Company isolation

Multi-tenant software earns trust by being specific about what separates one company from another, and by not relying on the interface to enforce it.

- Scope on every record: Every record carries the company it belongs to, and every request is resolved to a company before it reaches the data. There is no code path that returns a record outside your scope.
- Enforced on the server: Isolation is a property of the query rather than of the screen. Hiding a button is not a security control and this platform does not use it as one.
- Separable storage: A dedicated store per company is a configuration rather than a rewrite, because every data access goes through one internal interface. Organisations that require physical separation can have it.
- Departments within a company: A role scoped to a district cannot reach another district, which matters when the same company runs locations that should not see each other's customers.
- Transport security: All traffic is encrypted in transit with automatically renewed certificates, and the application follows a restrictive security header policy including a content security policy that prevents third party scripts from running in your session.
- Protected inbound callbacks: Requests the platform receives from carriers and providers are verified before they are acted on, so a forged callback cannot create a job or move money.

## Where your data physically sits, and who can see it

AlphaFlux runs on infrastructure the operator controls rather than on a shared public cloud, which changes the answer to a question more customers are asking: who else has this.

The short version is that your records are yours. They are not sold, not shared with advertisers, and not used to train anything. No third party script runs inside your session, because the interface serves everything it needs from the platform itself rather than loading it from an advertising or analytics network.

Backups are encrypted before they leave the machine that holds them. Where geographic separation is used for resilience, what travels is an encrypted artifact rather than a readable export.

Export is available at any time, in structured formats, without asking permission. A platform that makes leaving difficult is telling you what it thinks of you.


The right question is not whether the vendor says secure. It is who can see your customers, and what stops them.


## Rules for the AI features specifically

Agent access is the newest risk surface in business software, and it deserves specific answers rather than being folded into general security language.

- No path to the database: Agents act through the same validated operations your software uses. There is no route from a model to an arbitrary query.
- Nothing sensitive in a prompt: Agents receive the context they need to act. Payment details, carrier credentials and full customer records are not put in front of a model.
- Consequential actions need a person: Merging accounts, changing prices and bulk sending are presented as proposals for confirmation rather than performed on the model's own judgment.
- Attributed and reversible: Every agent action is recorded with its actor, so an automation that misbehaves is identified and stopped rather than argued about.

### Can you see my customer data?

The platform operator runs the infrastructure and can administer it. What that means in practice is governed by the agreement you have with the operator, and the platform supports running on infrastructure you control if that is the answer you need.

### Is my data used to train AI models?

No. Your records are not used to train anything. Where AI features run against a model, they receive the specific context required for the task, and the platform deliberately keeps customer identifying records and credentials out of that context.

### What happens if someone leaves the company?

Their access is removed, their sessions are destroyed, and anything they did remains attributed to them in the audit trail. Nothing they wrote is deleted, because a note about a customer is part of that customer's file.

### Do you use third party analytics on the platform?

No third party script runs inside a signed in session. The interface loads nothing from outside the platform, which is enforced by a content security policy rather than by a promise.

### Is there a compliance certification?

The platform is designed to the practices described on this page: least privilege, hashed credentials, full audit, encrypted transport and encrypted backups. Organisations with a specific regulatory requirement should raise it, because the architecture supports dedicated storage and regional hosting where that is what a rule demands.

# Your platform, your name, your customers

URL: https://alphaflux.net/white-label
Section: Platform

Five thousand a month buys the entire platform with every limit lifted, under your brand, on your domain, with the right to sell it to your own customers as your own product.

## What it is, plainly

Some companies do not want to buy software. They want to sell it. This is the version of AlphaFlux that makes that possible.

A franchise group wants one system across its locations, branded as the group. A managed service provider wants to offer field operations alongside what it already sells. A software company serving an industry wants an operations module without building one. An agency running marketing for service businesses wants to hand them the tool as part of the retainer.

In each case the platform is the same platform. What changes is whose name is on it, whose domain the customer signs in at, whose sending identity the email comes from, and who sets the pricing.

There is one flat monthly price, every module is included, no limits are applied, and the right to resell is part of it rather than a separate negotiation.

- Your brand everywhere a customer looks: Sign in page, console, mobile view, emails, invoices and the customer facing pages. No mention of AlphaFlux remains.
- Your domain: Customers sign in at your address. Certificates are issued and renewed automatically, so there is nothing to maintain.
- Your sending identity: Email leaves under your domain with your authentication records, so your reputation is built rather than borrowed.
- Your bundles and pricing: Define your own plans, your own limits and your own add ons from the module catalogue, and price them however you want.

## What arrives with it

Everything, with nothing held back for a higher tier.

- Every module, no limits: Phone and messaging, field operations, fleet and dispatch, scheduling and agreements, CRM, inventory and chemical tracking, billing, email marketing, marketing and growth, team collaboration, reporting and the advisor. Unlimited customers, locations, users, numbers and email volume.
- Agent access for your customers: The API, the command line and the agent protocol server are included, so your customers can automate against your platform the same way they could against ours.
- Separate companies under one operator: Run your own business and your customers' businesses side by side, each with its own records, users, branding and modules. New customers are provisioned without touching infrastructure.
- Your own catalogue: Because the module registry is data, you define which modules belong in which of your bundles and what each one costs. A customer buying from you sees your product line, not ours.
- Onboarding: Time with your team to get the first customers live, including how branding is applied, how workspaces are provisioned and how support should be handled.
- A named contact: One person who knows your account and your customers, rather than a ticket queue.

## Why the badge exists on every other plan

On every other plan, the customer facing pages carry a small line stating that the platform is provided by AlphaFlux. It is worth being direct about why, because it is an unusual thing to do.

It is how a host is discovered, and it is a large part of why a free plan can cost nothing. A company running happily on the free tier is, in a small way, paying for it by being an example. That keeps the free tier genuinely free rather than a trial with a countdown.

The badge is deliberately minimal. It appears only on the pages an end customer might see, never on the internal dashboards a company works in, and never in emails, invoices or anything a customer reads that is about money.

White label removes it entirely, along with every other trace, and hands over resale rights. That is the trade, stated plainly rather than buried in a footnote.


## How a white labelled deployment works

Setting it up is a configuration exercise, not a fork of the software.

- One line of configuration per brand: Brand name, marks, colour system, domain, sender identity and catalogue. Every one is a setting rather than a code change.
- You hold the accounts: You provision workspaces and manage them. Your customers see your support, because it is your product.
- Isolation is unchanged: Each of your customers is a company with its own records and its own scope, exactly as they would be under any other plan.
- Your own integrations: The interfaces are the same ones documented for developers, so your team can build on them under your own API surface if you want.
- Updates included: New modules and improvements land in your deployment. You are running the platform, not a frozen copy of one.
- Your customers' data stays theirs: The platform does not read your customers' data, does not use it to train anything, and does not market to them.

If your customers are signing in somewhere with someone else's name on it, you are renting an audience rather than building one.


## What white label changes


| Modules | By plan | All of them |
| Limits | By plan | None applied |
| Customers and locations | By plan | Unlimited |
| Users | By plan | Unlimited |
| Branding | AlphaFlux | !Yours |
| Sign in domain | Platform domain | !Your domain |
| Email sending identity | Platform | !Yours |
| Your own bundles and pricing | no | !Yes |
| Resale to your own customers | no | !Yes |
| Badge on customer facing pages | Present | !Removed |
| Support | Shared queue | Named contact |
| Setup | Self service | Onboarding included |

### Do I need technical staff to run it?

No. Branding, domains, sending identities and catalogues are configuration. Infrastructure is looked after, and certificates and updates are handled. Technical staff are only needed if you want to build custom integrations, and the interfaces for that are documented.

### Can I set my own prices and keep the difference?

Yes. You define your own bundles, your own limits and your own pricing, and you bill your customers directly. The platform does not see your customer relationships and does not sell to them.

### Is there a limit on how many customers I can have?

No. The white label plan carries no limits on customers, locations or users. The flat monthly price does not change as your customer base grows.

### Will my customers ever be contacted by AlphaFlux?

No. They are your customers. The platform does not market to them, does not email them, and does not use their data for anything beyond running their workspaces.

### Can I offer less than the whole platform to my customers?

Yes, and most operators do. You have every module available, and you decide which of them appear in which of your bundles. A customer of yours sees your product line, and you keep the rest in reserve for the next tier up.

### What if I want custom modules?

That is an enterprise conversation. Custom modules follow the same contract as the existing ones, which is what allows them to be added without disturbing anything already running.

# Every call answered, every text logged, nothing typed twice

URL: https://alphaflux.net/phone-and-messaging
Section: Modules

Your existing numbers on your own carrier account, with call handling per number, a voicemail inbox that reads, and a receptionist that answers before the second ring.

## The whole phone system, not just a dialler

A phone system that does not connect to the job it produced is a phone system that costs you a re-typing job every day.

- Numbers you control: Bring the numbers your customers already know, or buy new ones by area code. Each number gets its own behaviour.
- Texting that belongs to the account: Every inbound and outbound message lands on the customer timeline, not in a separate handset.
- Call handling per number: Greeting, ring through target, business hours and an after hours rule, configured per number rather than once for the whole company.
- A receptionist that books: The AI answers first, checks real capacity and puts the job on the schedule. Emergencies go straight to a person.
- A voicemail inbox that reads: Recordings, playback and transcripts in the console, with an unread count so nothing sits unheard for a week.
- Missed call text back: A missed call triggers a text within seconds, which is frequently the difference between a booked job and a lost one.

## How a call is handled, decision by decision

Every number carries its own rule set. Here is the order the platform works through when the phone rings.

- Answer: The call is answered immediately, so the caller never hears a ring they can hang up on.
- Receptionist or person: If the number has an AI receptionist attached, it is dialled first with a fifteen second window. If it does not answer, the human chain runs as if the AI had never been there. If the AI does answer, nobody's phone rings.
- Inside or outside hours: Business hours are set per number and per day. Inside hours the call rings through to the right person. Outside hours it follows the after hours rule you chose.
- The after hours rule: Three options per number: take a voicemail, forward to a number such as an answering service, or end the call politely. Which one is right depends on the business, so it is a setting rather than an assumption.
- Voicemail and text back: When a voicemail is taken it is transcribed, and a text back can be sent automatically so the caller knows they were heard rather than hoping.
- The record: The call, the transcript, the voicemail, any texts and the outcome all attach to the customer account. If the caller is new, the account is created by the call.

## The receptionist does the parts you would rather not staff

Answering the phone at nine at night is expensive to staff and cheap to automate, as long as it is done properly.

It identifies the caller, works out which office serves the address, checks whether the service described is one you offer, and books the visit against real capacity. It takes the details, leaves a complete record, and hands over to a person for anything that needs judgement.

It is bounded by the same rules your staff are: the service areas you actually cover, the capacity your technicians actually have, and a list of things it must never do. It does not quote a price that is not on your list, and it does not promise an exact arrival time.

The script lives inside AlphaFlux and is versioned, so changing how your business answers the phone is an edit rather than a ticket to a vendor.

- Right office, first time: The address is resolved against the areas each office covers before anything is booked.
- Knows what you sell: It can check the service against your catalogue, and deflect what you do not do instead of booking it.
- Books into real space: Availability comes from capacity rules, not from a guess, so the schedule is never oversold.
- Escalates properly: An emergency is routed to a person immediately, and a sales call is answered from a script.

## Messaging done to carrier standards

Business texting has rules. The platform handles the registration and the compliance so messages arrive.

- Brand and campaign registration: The registration work that carriers require before application to person messaging is supported in the console, with the status of each registration visible rather than hidden.
- Opt out handling: A customer who replies to stop is suppressed from future sends automatically. That applies equally to a person sending and to an agent sending.
- Message logging on the account: Every message in and out is recorded against the customer timeline, with the number it came from and the person or agent who sent it.
- Deliverability signals: Failed and undelivered messages are surfaced rather than silently dropped, because a text that never arrived is worse than one never sent.
- More than one sender identity: Alphanumeric sender identifiers, short codes and messaging services are all manageable from the same place on the larger plans.

A missed call is a lead that has already decided to call you. It should almost never be lost.


## What the phone module includes


| Phone numbers | 1 | 2 to 5 | 25 |
| Text messaging | yes | yes | yes |
| Voicemail with transcript | yes | yes | yes |
| Missed call text back | yes | yes | yes |
| Per number call handling | Basic | yes | yes |
| AI receptionist | no | Growth and above | yes |
| Recording and transcription | no | yes | yes |
| Registration and compliance tools | no | yes | yes |

### Do I have to port my numbers?

No, and in most cases you should not. You can connect the carrier account you already have so your existing numbers keep working and stay yours. Porting is only needed if you want the number managed under a different carrier account.

### Can the AI receptionist take a payment?

It does not take card details on a call, and that is deliberate. It can book the work, take the details and leave a record, and payment is collected through the normal invoicing route where the customer has a receipt and you have a record.

### What happens if the AI does not understand the caller?

It hands over. If it cannot place the call in one of the categories it handles, or if the caller asks for a person, or if it is an emergency, the call moves to a human by the rule you set for that number.

### Can I listen to calls later?

Recordings and transcriptions are available on the plans that include them, attached to the customer account rather than sitting in a separate call list.

### Does this work for a company with several offices?

Each office can have its own numbers and its own call handling, and the receptionist resolves callers to the correct office by address. A central number can also route by the caller's location.

# The whole day, from the first job to the proof it was done

URL: https://alphaflux.net/field-operations
Section: Modules

One object moves from booked to dispatched to on site to complete to paid. The office sees it, the technician sees it, the customer sees a window, and the proof is attached before anyone leaves.

## What the field operation gets

The point is that the office and the truck are looking at the same thing at the same time.

- Jobs with a real record: Customer, service, technician, time window, price, duration, notes, photos and signature on one object.
- A dispatch map: Today's work and every technician's last known position on one map, so a late job is visible before it becomes a call.
- Day routes that make sense: Sequence a technician's stops, with the total distance stated and the option to re-optimise before the day starts.
- Proof of work: Photo, signature, timestamp and location captured at the job, attached to the record and available to the customer.
- Technicians as real people: Skills, home base, schedule and availability, so work is assigned to someone who can actually do it.
- Check in and out: A technician checks in when they arrive and out when they leave, which is what makes the mileage and the time on site real numbers.

## The job lifecycle, and what is enforced at each step

Status is not a label someone types. It is a state the platform checks, and a transition that is not allowed is refused with the ones that are.

- Booked: The job is created with a customer, a service and a time. The address is placed on the map so the job can be routed, and the booking is checked against real capacity before it is confirmed.
- Assigned: A technician is chosen. Skills and service area are respected, so work does not land on someone who cannot do it or who is hours away.
- Dispatched: The technician has the job and the customer has a window. If the day moves, the affected customers are notified rather than left waiting.
- On site: Checked in, with the arrival time recorded from the technician's device. This is where the time on site and the mileage start being real numbers rather than estimates.
- Complete: The work is done and the proof is attached. If the job type requires a photo or a signature, the job cannot be closed without one, so the file is complete at the moment of closure rather than a week later.
- Billed: The completed job carries its parts, its labour and its notes into the invoice. Nothing is re-keyed from a paper form, and the price was agreed when the job was booked.

## A technician view built for one hand and bad signal

The field view runs in the phone's browser and installs to the home screen. It is designed for a technician standing in a crawlspace, not for someone at a desk.

Today's jobs, in order, with the address and the customer's notes. One button to check in, one to check out, one to attach a photo, one to take a signature. The next job is one tap away and the driving directions open in the phone's own maps.

Status changes made without a signal are queued and applied in order when the connection returns, so a technician in a basement does not lose the arrival time or the completion.

Nothing on the screen needs two hands, and nothing needs reading at arm's length in the sun. That is the whole design brief for this view.

- The day, in order: Stops sequenced, addresses and customer notes attached, and the next stop one tap away.
- Capture from the phone: Photos and signatures taken on the device and attached to the job rather than texted to the office.
- Location, when it helps: Check in and check out report a position, which makes arrival times and distance travelled real rather than reconstructed.
- Offline that recovers: Changes made with no signal are held and applied in order, so the record stays correct even from a basement.

## Why the routing numbers say straight line

Route sequencing measures straight line distance between stops, and the interface says so. That is not a limitation to be embarrassed about, it is a decision about honesty: a dispatcher who catches a system claiming road accuracy it does not have stops trusting every other number it produces.

Straight line ordering gets a day of eight to fifteen stops very close to the right sequence, which is the part that saves the fuel. Where road distance genuinely changes the answer, the platform supports a road based routing engine as a configuration rather than pretending.

The same rule applies to arrival estimates. An estimate is labelled as an estimate, and the platform would rather show a range it can stand behind than a precise time it cannot.


A job is not finished when the work is done. It is finished when the record, the proof and the invoice agree.


## Field operations by plan


| Jobs and customers | 20 customers | 250 customers | 1,000 customers | 5,000 and above |
| Technicians | 1 | 3 | 10 | 25 and above |
| Dispatch map | no | Basic | yes | yes |
| Day route sequencing | no | no | yes | yes |
| Proof of work | no | no | yes | yes |
| Technician mobile view | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Service agreements | no | yes | yes | yes |

### Can I assign the same technician to two jobs at once?

The platform will let you if you force it, but it will tell you first. Booking is checked against the capacity rules you set at the office, the area and the individual level, and an override is recorded so it is visible later rather than invisible forever.

### Does the technician need a company phone?

No. The field view is a web page that installs to the home screen of whatever phone the technician carries, including a personal one. Nothing needs to be installed from an app store.

### How does the platform handle a job that runs long?

The remaining stops for that day can be re-sequenced, and the affected customers can be notified with a new window. Because the customer's window comes from the same record the dispatcher is moving, there is no second list to keep in step.

### Is there a paper option?

A completed job can be printed or exported with its photos, signature and notes, which is what most companies need when a customer or an insurer asks for documentation.

### Can customers see where the technician is?

Yes, on the plans that include tracking. The customer receives a link that shows their own job and nothing else, and the link expires when the job is done.

# Watch the work move on a map, run it on a board

URL: https://alphaflux.net/fleet
Section: Modules

A dispatcher's screen that shows the truth at a glance: every order, every vehicle, every technician, the route each one is on and the customer watching their own technician arrive.

## The dispatcher's screen

Dispatch is two questions asked all day: what is happening right now, and who should take the next one. Both should be answerable without opening four things.

- A live fleet map: Orders, technicians, vehicles, routes, service areas and geofences on one map, updating as the day moves rather than when someone refreshes.
- An order board: Every order as a card, every stage as a column. Drag a card to move it and the record moves with it.
- Geofences that notice: Draw an arrival zone and the platform marks the order on site when the technician crosses it, so nobody has to tap a button in a driveway.
- Arrival estimates: Remaining distance and the technician's recent pace produce a window, labelled as an estimate and updated as the day changes.
- Vehicles and fleets: Track trucks and trailers as assets with their own status, capacity, assigned driver and service history, not just as a name in a spreadsheet.
- Customer tracking: Send a link that shows one order's live status, and only that order. It expires when the work is done.

## A card is the whole order, not a summary of one

Opening a card on the board gives you everything the order carries, and moving it is a real transition the server validates.

- Unassigned (07:10)
- Assigned (07:22)
- En route (07:41)
- On site (08:03)
- Complete (08:48)

## The board cannot invent a state

A board that lets anyone drag a card anywhere is a board that quietly corrupts the record. Here, the server decides what is legal and the board only offers what it is told.

Every order type has a defined set of stages and a defined set of moves between them. When a card is dropped, the change is sent to the server as a transition. If it is allowed, it is applied and written to the order's history. If it is not, it is refused with the moves that are actually available, and the card returns to where it was.

That is what makes the board trustworthy rather than decorative. The same discipline that governs the technicians' status changes governs the dispatcher's screen, so a card that says complete really is complete, with the proof attached and the invoice following.

Every move is recorded with who did it, whether that was a person or an agent, and when. The order's history is not reconstructed later from memory. It was written down as it happened.

- Your stages, not ours: Define the order types you actually run and the stages each one passes through, with the fields each stage requires.
- Rules attached to stages: A stage can require a photo, a signature, a part or a note before the order is allowed to leave it.
- History as it happened: Every transition is appended with actor, time and position, giving the timeline and the audit trail from the same records.
- Automation on top: Transitions can trigger the next thing: notify the customer, raise the invoice, order the part, or ask a person to look.

## What is on the map

Layers can be turned on and off so a dispatcher sees the district, not the world.

- Orders: Every open order for the day, coloured by stage, so unassigned work is visible as a cluster rather than as a list to read.
- Technicians and vehicles: Last known position with a freshness indicator, so a stale ping shows as stale rather than as a truck parked in a field for an hour.
- Routes: The sequenced route for a technician, with the remaining stops and the distance left, so a dispatcher can see whether the day is recoverable.
- Service areas and zones: The areas you cover, drawn as polygons and used for routing, capacity and pricing rather than only for colour on a screen.
- Geofences: Arrival zones, restricted areas and site boundaries, each with a behaviour such as marking arrival or flagging a deviation.
- Places and customers: Saved locations, including multi unit buildings, so a job resolves to the right building, floor or unit rather than to a street address.

## For operations that run trucks, not just technicians

The same records serve a plumbing company with four vans and a fleet operation with trailers and depots.

- Trailers and equipment: Towed and portable assets tracked in their own right, with connections to vehicles that change over time rather than being overwritten.
- Maintenance schedules: Service intervals by vehicle or by hours, work orders, parts used and warranty records, so maintenance is planned rather than reactive.
- Fuel and cost per mile: Fuel records and running costs per vehicle, so the cost of a route is a number rather than an intuition.
- Telematics: Connect a telematics provider and vehicle positions and sensor data arrive without anyone's phone being involved.
- Manifests: Group orders onto a manifest for a run, so a multi stop delivery or a bulk collection is one object rather than twenty.
- Operations reporting: On time percentage, jobs per technician, distance and utilisation, out of the records the dispatcher is already using.

A dispatcher should be able to answer what happened today without asking anyone.


## Fleet and dispatch by plan


| Order board | yes | yes | yes |
| Custom order types and stages | yes | yes | yes |
| Live map | Basic | yes | yes |
| Geofences and arrival detection | no | yes | yes |
| Arrival estimates | no | yes | yes |
| Vehicles and trailers | no | yes | yes |
| Telematics connections | no | yes | yes |
| Customer tracking links | no | yes | yes |
| Unlimited everything | no | no | yes |

### How often do positions update?

Positions are reported by the technician's device as they move, and the dispatcher's map updates without a refresh. The interface shows how fresh each position is, because a map that hides a ten minute old position is worse than one that admits it.

### Can I use my own map provider?

The map is served through the platform, and no third party script runs in your browser or tracks your customers. Where a commercial basemap is preferred it can be configured, and the customer tracking page continues to render through the platform.

### Do I need telematics hardware?

No. Positions come from the technicians' devices by default, which works on day one with no hardware. Telematics is for operations that want vehicle data without depending on a phone, and it can be added later.

### Can a customer see where the technician is without seeing anything else?

Yes. A tracking link is scoped to one order and shows only that order's status and arrival window. It carries no customer data, it cannot be used to browse anything else, and it expires when the work is complete.

### Does the board work for a company with several districts?

Yes, and the districts are enforced rather than filtered. A dispatcher scoped to one district sees that district's board and map, and the restriction is applied in the query rather than by hiding things on screen.

# Fill the calendar without overselling the day

URL: https://alphaflux.net/scheduling
Section: Modules

Booking that checks the real limits of the day before it confirms, and recurring agreements that generate their own visits for the whole term without anyone remembering to renew them.

## Capacity is the limit nobody can see until it is broken

Most companies discover they oversold a day when a technician calls in from the road. Booking against a rule instead of a feeling is what stops it.

Every booking is checked against the capacity rules that apply to it before it is confirmed. The rules can be set at the office level, the area level or the individual technician level, and per weekday, because Tuesday is rarely Saturday.

When two rules apply, the more specific one wins, and the narrower limit is checked as well as the wider one. A technician with a light day inside a busy area still has a personal limit, and the platform checks both rather than picking one.

A booking that does not fit is refused with the reason named, and the platform offers the next day that does fit. Overriding it is possible, and the override is recorded with who did it, because a person sometimes genuinely knows better than the rule.

- Limits that match reality: Jobs, minutes or both, at office, area or technician level, set per day of the week.
- Areas, not guesswork: Service areas are grouped from postcodes, so coverage and capacity are expressed the way the business already describes itself.
- Availability on request: Ask what a given day can still take and get an answer, which is what makes online booking and agent booking safe.
- Overrides are visible: A forced booking is allowed, recorded and flagged, so the exception is documented rather than quietly absorbed.

## Recurring work, handled properly

Recurring service is the backbone of a service business and the part most software handles worst.

- Agreements that generate visits: Define a frequency and a term and the platform creates every visit for the term, each with its own date, price and technician.
- Dates that stay honest: A visit on the 31st stays on the 31st, and clamps sensibly in a short month rather than drifting forward forever.
- Recurring revenue you can trust: Monthly recurring revenue is calculated from the actual charges on the agreement, not from a projection or a guess.
- Changes without damage: Moving a schedule cancels and regenerates future visits and leaves completed work exactly where it was.
- Reminders that go out: Upcoming visits trigger a confirmation before the technician is dispatched, so a wasted trip becomes a rebooked one.
- A book you can read: One view of the recurring book: how many agreements, what they are worth a month, and which ones are up for renewal.

## How a booking is checked

The order the platform works through when something is being put on the calendar, whether by a person, a customer or an agent.

- Does this area accept work: The address is resolved to a service area. A postcode outside every area you cover is declined at the point of booking rather than after a technician is dispatched.
- Is there capacity that day: The technician's limit, the area's limit and the office's limit are all checked. The most specific rule wins, and the tighter constraint applies.
- Does the technician fit the work: Skills and certifications are checked, so a job that requires a particular licence does not land on someone who does not hold it.
- Is the travel realistic: The location is checked against the rest of that technician's day, so the schedule does not contain a stop that is physically impossible.
- Is it confirmed or proposed: A booking that fits is confirmed and the customer is notified. One that does not is declined with the reason and the nearest day that works.

## The appointment is the promise, the visit is the work

A recurring agreement is not a list of dates in a spreadsheet. It is an agreement with a term, a frequency, a price and a start date, and the platform derives every visit from it.

That distinction matters when something changes. Because each visit knows which agreement produced it and which visit number it is, regenerating a schedule is safe to run twice, and a visit that has already been completed is never disturbed by a change to the future.

It also means the money and the work cannot drift apart. The recurring revenue a plan reports comes from the same agreements that generate the visits, so the number on the dashboard and the work on the calendar are the same fact.


## Scheduling by plan


| Job booking | yes | yes | yes |
| Service areas | 1 | 2 | 5 and above |
| Capacity rules | no | yes | yes |
| Availability lookup | no | yes | yes |
| Service agreements | no | yes | yes |
| Automated visit generation | no | yes | yes |
| Appointment reminders | no | yes | yes |
| Recurring revenue reporting | no | yes | yes |

### Can customers book themselves?

Yes. Because availability is a real answer rather than a calendar someone maintains by hand, a customer facing booking page can only offer slots that genuinely exist, which removes the confirmation round trip entirely.

### What if I need to squeeze in an emergency?

Force it. The platform will tell you the day is over its limit, and if you proceed it books the job and records that the limit was overridden and by whom. Emergencies happen, and the platform is built to accommodate them without losing the record.

### How does a change to an agreement affect visits already done?

It does not touch them. Completed and past work is left exactly as it is. Only future visits that have not happened are cancelled and regenerated under the new schedule.

### Can different services have different frequencies?

Yes, each agreement carries its own service and frequency. A company can run quarterly pest treatments on one agreement and a monthly maintenance contract on another for the same customer.

### What time zone are appointments in?

Times are stored unambiguously and displayed in the company's local time, so a business operating across states sees its own day rather than a server's.

# The customer record the phone system and the truck both point at

URL: https://alphaflux.net/crm
Section: Modules

A CRM that is not a separate list of people. It is the same account the call came into, the job was booked against, the invoice was raised for and the campaign was sent to.

## What the customer record holds

Everything about one account in one place, because the alternative is four places that disagree.

- Contacts and accounts: People and the companies or properties they belong to, with multiple sites under one account where that is how the relationship works.
- A pipeline that reflects your sales: Lead, contacted, quoted, won or lost, with the stages and values that make sense for how you actually sell.
- One timeline per account: Calls, texts, emails, notes, jobs, invoices, payments and changes in a single chronological feed.
- Notes with mentions: Write a note on an account and mention a colleague or another account. The mention becomes a notification, not a message that gets lost.
- Tags that are a system: A shared tag vocabulary with colour and category, applied in bulk, so accounts can be filtered the same way by everyone.
- Duplicates found and merged: The platform proposes merges when a phone number, an email or a name matches, shows the evidence that linked them, and merges only when a person approves.

## Teams, territories and who can see what

Selling and servicing a large account is rarely one person's job. The record supports the whole team without everyone seeing everything.

- Account teams: Attach the people who work on an account with a role on that account: who sells it, who services it, who handles the billing, who is the escalation point. Each one is named on the record rather than inferred from who happened to touch it last.
- Territories and assignment: Define territories by area, postcode or service line and let an account be assigned automatically when it arrives, so a new lead lands with the right person without a manual sorting step.
- Roles that scope access: A role is a set of permissions. Scoped to a territory or a district, it means a salesperson sees their own patch and a manager sees all of it, and neither has to be maintained by hand.
- Sharing on the account: An account can be shared with specific people or a whole team, so covering for someone on leave does not mean sharing a login.
- Activity that is attributable: Every call, note, job and message records who did it, whether that was a person, an agent or an import, and when.

## Who sold it, and who gets paid for it

Three different people can be responsible for one sale, and collapsing them into a single owner column is how commission disputes start.

AlphaFlux records three separate roles on an account. Who sold it, which is the person owed commission. Who services it, which is the technician or team who keeps it. And who booked it, which distinguishes a lead that came from a person from one that came from an agent or an import.

Splits are recorded in basis points and must total exactly one hundred percent before they can be saved. A split that does not add up is not a rounding problem to be tolerated, it is a commission error waiting to be discovered at the worst moment.

Attribution history is append-only. When ownership changes, the previous entry is superseded rather than overwritten, so a payout made in March can still be explained in September, and revenue an agent generated stays separable from revenue a person generated.

- Splits that must total: The platform refuses a split that does not add to one hundred percent, in basis points, before it is stored.
- History that is not overwritten: Ownership changes supersede the prior entry. Nothing is erased, so an old payout is always explicable.
- Agent revenue, separated: Revenue booked by an agent is a distinct category, which is how you find out whether the automation is actually paying for itself.
- Reports by source and by person: Who sold what, over what period, at what commission rate, from which lead source.

If two systems know a customer, one of them is wrong and you will find out at the worst possible time.


## CRM by plan


| Contacts and accounts | 20 | 250 | 1,000 | 5,000 and above |
| Pipeline and stages | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Account timeline | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Tags | Basic | yes | yes | yes |
| Notes and mentions | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Duplicate detection and merge | no | yes | yes | yes |
| Sales attribution and splits | no | yes | yes | yes |
| Teams and territories | no | no | yes | yes |

### Do I have to move my contacts in from somewhere else?

You can import from a spreadsheet, or connect an existing field service account and read it live while you decide what to move. Many companies run both for a period, which is a deliberate option rather than a leap of faith.

### What happens if two people create the same customer?

The platform notices and proposes a merge, showing which signal linked the two records, whether that was a shared phone number, a shared email or the same name and address. Nothing merges automatically, and a merge can be reversed if it turns out to be wrong.

### Can I see an account's whole history in one place?

Yes. The account timeline mixes calls, texts, emails, notes, jobs, payments and agent activity in one chronological feed, with filtering so a support question can be answered without reading a year of unrelated activity.

### How does commission work for a team sale?

Splits are recorded per person in basis points and must total one hundred percent. Payouts are computed from those splits and snapshotted, so a rate change in the future does not silently rewrite what someone was owed in the past.

### Does the CRM know about field work?

It is the same record. A job booked by a technician or an agent appears on the account timeline, and a customer's job history is visible from the account without switching modules.
